claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5 at% interstitial carbon to MnNiSi improves fracture toughness and ductility.
Mechanical alloying followed by annealing at 973 K for 12 h achieves interstitial carbon incorporation.
Interstitial carbon segregates to MnNiSi grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary carbon increases grain-boundary cohesion.
Grain-boundary carbon impedes crack-tip propagation.
Carbon raises grain-boundary cohesion energy.
Carbon increases dislocation-emission resistance near grain boundaries.
The proposed carbon addition does not significantly strain the lattice parameters responsible for the magnetostructural transition.
The undoped MnNiSi baseline has a fracture toughness of approximately 2.0 MPa·m^0.5.
The undoped MnNiSi baseline has a flexural failure strain of approximately 1.6%.
The undoped MnNiSi baseline has a peak magnetic entropy change of approximately 35 J·kg^-1·K^-1 under a 5 T field change at 300 K.
Carbon doping increases fracture toughness by at least 30%, from approximately 2.0 to at least 2.6 MPa·m^0.5.
Carbon doping increases flexural failure strain by at least 25%, from approximately 1.6% to at least 2.0%.
The carbon-doped alloy retains at least 90% of the undoped peak magnetic entropy change under a 5 T field change.
The retained peak magnetic entropy change is at least 31 J·kg^-1·K^-1.
The proposed effects hold for carbon contents between 0.3 and 0.7 at% when annealed at 973 K for 12 h.
Outside the stated carbon-content range, carbon segregation behavior and the magnetic transition may change.
Carbon solubility and spatial distribution vary with processing.
Variation in carbon solubility and distribution affects the magnitude of mechanical improvements.
Variation in carbon solubility and distribution affects retention of magnetocaloric performance.

contradictions.description: The baseline is specified as arc-melted and homogenized at 1173 K for 48 h, whereas the doped material is mechanically alloyed and annealed at 973 K for 12 h. The experiment nevertheless calls for doped and undoped samples to receive identical melting and annealing protocols, leaving the actual baseline comparison inconsistent and potentially confounded by processing.

The predicted toughness increase is at least 30%, but the hypothesis is declared falsified only below a 15% increase. Results between 15% and 30% would violate the quantitative prediction without meeting the stated falsification rule.
